Skew Normal Log-CDF Derivatives

Source: R/cdf_skewnormal_higher.R
distrib_grad_cdf.SkewNormal1Distrib.Rd

The derivatives are in closed form at every order from one to four, in the shape as well as in the location and the scale. With \(z = (q-\mu)/\sigma\) the distribution function is \(\Phi(z) - 2T(z,\alpha)\), and Owen's \(T\) has elementary partial derivatives in both arguments, so the integral in its definition is differentiated away at the first order and never has to be differentiated again. The location and the scale then enter only through \(z\), by the same chain rule that the other location-scale families use.

Arguments

distrib

A SkewNormal1Distrib object, from skewnormal1_distrib().

q

A numeric vector of quantiles.

theta

A named list with components mu, sigma (positive) and alpha (any sign); each is a numeric vector of length 1 or n.

lower.tail

A single logical, TRUE by default; TRUE selects the lower tail and FALSE the upper tail.

log

A single logical, TRUE by default; TRUE selects the derivatives of the log probability and FALSE those of the probability.

...

Unused, and accepted so that the signature matches the generic's.

Value

A named list of numeric vectors of the requested order, keyed as deriv_names(distrib@params, order): three components for the gradient, six for the Hessian, ten at order 3 and fifteen at order 4.

Accuracy

The derivatives are closed forms. A product stencil on the same distribution function loses accuracy as the order grows, by one or two digits per order.

Relation to the Student t and the pseudo-Huber

The shape components of the skew normal are closed through the elementary partial derivatives of Owen's T given above. The Student t, the pseudo-Huber and the skew t have no closed derivative in a shape parameter; their shape components are integrals of the density's own derivatives, taken by the compiled rule.

Notation

\(\mu\) is the location, \(\sigma > 0\) the scale, \(\alpha\) the shape, \(z = (q-\mu)/\sigma\), \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function and \(T\) Owen's T.

See also

sn_cdf_std_derivs() and sn_cdf_deriv_k() for the construction; distrib_grad_cdf.SkewTDistrib(), which integrates its shape derivatives by the compiled rule; skewnormal1_distrib().

Examples

d <- skewnormal1_distrib()
q <- c(-1, 0.5, 2)
th <- list(mu = 0.3, sigma = 1.2, alpha = 2)

# The location component is exact, the density itself.
all.equal(distrib_grad_cdf(d, q, th, log = FALSE)$mu,
          -distrib_pdf(d, q, th))
#> [1] TRUE

# At shape zero the family is Gaussian, and its location and scale
# derivatives agree with the Gaussian's.
g0 <- distrib_grad_cdf(d, q, list(mu = 0.3, sigma = 1.2, alpha = 0),
                       log = FALSE)
gg <- distrib_grad_cdf(gaussian1_distrib(), q, list(mu = 0.3, sigma = 1.2),
                       log = FALSE)
max(abs(g0$mu - gg$mu))
#> [1] 2.775558e-17

# The number of components is three, six, ten and fifteen as the order rises.
lengths(list(distrib_grad_cdf(d, q, th),
             distrib_hess_cdf(d, q, th),
             distrib_deriv3_cdf(d, q, th),
             distrib_deriv4_cdf(d, q, th)))
#> [1]  3  6 10 15
